title: Rude Q&A: Stress-testing your startup with a brutal devil's advocate
summary: Jason Cohen borrows Scott Berkun's "Rude Q&A": write down the nastiest, smartest, even unfair questions about your company, then answer them. The exercise tests your ideas and forces sharper messaging, target customer and features. He gives a starter list of startup questions and a worked answer about why his own blog should exist.

principles.text: Write a Rude Q&A: the questions you least want to hear about your work, then answer them as practice for pitching and raising money.
principles.quote: What would the meanest, nastiest, but smartest people in the world grill you on when you show your work?

principles.text: Grilling yourself does more than test the idea: it forces specific messaging, customer profile, differentiation and feature set.
principles.quote: It's not just about testing the mettle of your ideas, it also forces you to refine and clarify your marketing messages, your target customer profile, and your feature set.

principles.text: Include unfair questions and ones built on wrong assumptions, since reporters, clients and the public will ask them.
principles.quote: Make sure to include questions that are unfair or based on erroneous information.

principles.text: Answer unfair questions politely and maturely, refuting the false assumptions without being dismissive.
principles.quote: They also need to carefully refute assumptions in the questions without being dismissive.

principles.text: Make generic tough questions specific to your own business, with the real comparisons and competitors that make it hurt.
principles.quote: These are generic; you'll need to come up with more specific attacks.

principles.text: Being dissatisfied with some of your answers is a good sign; keep looking for answers and discuss the hard ones with others.
principles.quote: Don't get discouraged if you're not happy with all your answers. That's a good sign--it means you're being honest about the exercise and you're not yet satisfied.
